analysis.one_liner: Gives FDA power to order safety studies of risky drugs and shields whistleblowers who report problems.
analysis.headline: A drug-safety bill from Rep. Markey with a Democratic cosponsor was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2007 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Health and Human Services Secretary order a drugmaker to run safety studies of an already-approved drug when new evidence raises concerns, and to restrict how the drug is distributed or advertised while the study runs. Drugs approved on a fast track for serious illnesses would carry warning labels and face restricted advertising until their required follow-up studies were done; a company that failed to complete a study could face civil penalties of up to 100% of its profits from the drug, and drugs whose studies came back inconclusive could be pulled from the market. The bill would also make it illegal to retaliate against FDA employees and contractors who report safety problems, guarantee FDA scientists the right to publish their findings, and require a public summary of the scientific basis for each drug approval within 48 hours.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients taking approved drugs, especially those on drugs approved through the accelerated process for serious or life-threatening illnesses, would get stronger follow-up safety checks and clearer warning labels. FDA employees and contractors who report censorship or falsified science would gain enforceable whistleblower protections with reinstatement, back pay, and punitive damages [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary could order a drugmaker to conduct postmarket studies within 30 days of evidence of a significant safety or effectiveness problem, and could restrict distribution, limit advertising, or condition use on special medical procedures while the study runs [S2] [S3].

Drugs approved on the accelerated track for serious or life-threatening illnesses would have to run required postmarket studies, bear labels disclosing that approval is conditional, and face restricted direct-to-consumer advertising until the studies are complete; a study not finished within five years is presumed inconclusive and the drug would be withdrawn except for patients who previously benefited and consent [S3].
Violations could carry civil penalties of up to 100% of the sponsor's gross profits from the drug, or up to 300% if a consumer is harmed [S3].

The bill would prohibit retaliation against FDA employees and contractors who report violations or suppressed science, with remedies including reinstatement, back pay, attorney fees, and punitive damages up to $5 million or triple damages, plus criminal fines and up to 10 years in prison [S3].

FDA scientists could not be directed to censor or suppress research, could publish in peer-reviewed journals, could present dissenting views to advisory committees, and each new drug approval would require a published summary of the scientific basis for the decision within 48 hours [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drugmakers, especially those selling drugs approved through the accelerated process, would bear the cost of mandatory postmarket studies, restrictions on distribution and advertising, misbranding liability for noncompliance, and civil penalties tied to gross profits [S3].

drawbacks.text: While a required study is underway, the Secretary could restrict distribution of a drug to certain facilities or physicians, which could delay access for patients with serious illnesses who need the drug [S3].

A drug whose required study was not completed within five years would be presumed inconclusive and pulled from general sale, which patients and some physicians might contest when the drug appeared to be helping people [S3].

The compliance burden and the penalty structure, including penalties of up to 100% of gross profits, would fall on drugmakers and could make companies more cautious about seeking accelerated approval for drugs for serious illnesses [S3].

The required approval summary would name every FDA official who participated in the decision and describe internal disagreements, which could make agency scientists more hesitant to voice candid views during review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-safety benefits are substantial: earlier safety studies, real restrictions on risky drugs, and protected whistleblowers inside the FDA. The main costs are slower access to conditionally approved drugs during follow-up studies and heavier compliance burdens on drugmakers. For people with serious illnesses waiting on fast-tracked drugs, the access tradeoff is real but the bill preserved case-by-case continued access with informed consent for patients already benefiting from a drug pulled for inconclusive results [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee from late February 2007 until the Congress ended in January 2009, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the SAFE Drug Act on February 16, 2007, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On February 27, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill had one cosponsor, a House Democrat [S4].

The bill would have given the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to order postmarket safety studies, restrict distribution and advertising of drugs under review, and impose civil penalties of up to 100% of a sponsor's gross profits for violations [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers, particularly sponsors of conditionally approved drugs, avoided the mandatory postmarket studies, distribution and advertising restrictions, and profit-linked penalties the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Rep. Edward J. Markey
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE Drug Act on February 16, 2007 and delivered introductory remarks on the measure

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over drug safety law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Health and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled in the 110th Congress

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows only that support was confined to one party, with no roll-call to measure broader backing.

industries.note: The bill would have required postmarket safety studies, allowed FDA to restrict distribution and advertising of drugs under review, mandated public conditional-approval labels for fast-tracked drugs, and imposed civil penalties of up to 100% of gross profits for violations. Its costs fall on the companies; its benefits to patients run opposite to the industry's interest in avoiding restrictions on profitable drugs [S2] [S3].

The Secretary could restrict direct-to-consumer advertisements for any drug under a postmarket study order, and advertising would be restricted for all conditionally approved drugs until follow-up studies were complete, cutting promotional revenue [S3].
